title: Sign-in, passwords & accounts
blurb: Forgotten passwords, locked accounts, two-step sign-in, Windows Hello and Touch ID.

remedies.title: I forgot my password
remedies.why: Which reset works depends on the account: a work/school account, a Microsoft or Apple account, or a local account on this computer.

steps.text: Work or school account: use your organisation's self-service reset (Microsoft: aka.ms/sspr) or call IT.
Microsoft account (Outlook.com, Hotmail): on the sign-in screen choose "I forgot my password", or account.live.com/password/reset from another device.
Local Windows account: answer the security questions on the sign-in screen, or use a password reset disk.
Mac: after a few wrong tries, the login window offers to reset with your Apple Account or recovery key.
Afterwards, update the password on your phone and other devices so they don't lock the account.

remedies.escalate: IT can reset work passwords after checking who you are.

remedies.title: My account is locked
symptoms: referenced account is currently locked out
remedies.why: Too many wrong passwords, often from an old password still saved on a phone or another device.

steps.text: Wait: many locks lift after 15–30 minutes.
Find the device with the old password: phone mail app, a second computer, a mapped drive or Wi-Fi profile. Update or remove it.
Don't keep retrying; each wrong try can extend the lock.

remedies.escalate: IT can unlock work accounts and see which device keeps sending the wrong password.

remedies.title: After changing my password, everything asks for it again
symptoms: after password change outlook teams onedrive
remedies.why: Apps and devices remember the old password until you sign in again.

steps.text: Lock and unlock the computer (Windows+L / Ctrl+⌘+Q) while on the work network or VPN, so it learns the new password.
Sign in again in Outlook, Teams and OneDrive when they ask.
Update saved passwords: Credential Manager › Windows Credentials.
Update saved passwords in Keychain Access, or delete the old entries.
Update your phone's mail and Wi-Fi so it doesn't lock the account.

remedies.title: Two-step sign-in (MFA) code or approval doesn't arrive
remedies.why: The phone has no data, notifications are off, the clock is wrong, or the authenticator was set up on an old phone.

steps.text: Open the Authenticator app yourself; approvals often wait inside the app even without a notification.
Use the code shown in the app instead (choose "Use a verification code").
Check the phone's date and time are automatic; codes depend on the clock.
New phone? Move accounts with the app's backup, or sign in at mysignins.microsoft.com / your provider's security page from a working device to add the new phone.

remedies.escalate: Lost or replaced phone with no backup: IT (or the provider's account recovery) must reset your two-step sign-in.

remedies.title: Windows Hello PIN, fingerprint or face sign-in not working
symptoms: something happened and your pin isn't available
remedies.why: The Hello data got damaged, the sensor driver failed, or the PIN was reset by your organisation.

steps.text: Sign in with your password instead (Sign-in options under the PIN box).
Settings › Accounts › Sign-in options › PIN › I forgot my PIN, or Remove and set it up again.
Set up fingerprint or face again in the same place; clean the sensor or camera.
Check the sensor in Device Manager › Biometric devices.

remedies.title: Touch ID doesn't work
remedies.why: Dry or wet fingers, a dirty sensor, or a fingerprint that needs adding again. After a restart, your password is always needed once.

steps.text: After a restart, type your password once; Touch ID works after that.
Clean the sensor and your finger.
Delete and add the fingerprint again; add the same finger twice for better matching.

remedies.title: Mac keeps asking for the keychain password
symptoms: accountsd wants to use the login keychain
remedies.why: The login keychain still uses an old password after the Mac password changed.

steps.text: Type your old Mac password if you know it; that unlocks and updates it.
Otherwise Keychain Access › Settings › Reset Default Keychains (saved passwords in it are lost, iCloud Keychain passwords stay).

remedies.title: I think my account was hacked
remedies.why: Someone got your password (phishing, reuse from a leaked site, or malware).

steps.text: From a device you trust, change the password now, and anywhere you used the same one.
Turn on two-step sign-in (MFA).
Check sign-in activity and sign out all other sessions (Microsoft: account.microsoft.com/security; Google: myaccount.google.com/security; Apple: Devices list).
Check mail rules and forwarding: attackers add rules that hide or forward your mail.
Warn contacts not to open odd messages from you.

remedies.escalate: For a work account, tell IT immediately; they can block the attacker and check what was accessed.

remedies.title: BitLocker asks for a recovery key
remedies.why: BitLocker saw a change (firmware update, new hardware, a dock at startup, BIOS settings) and wants proof it's still you.

steps.text: Unplug docks and USB devices and restart once; sometimes that's all it was.
Find the key: aka.ms/myrecoverykey on another device, sign in with the account used on this PC (personal Microsoft account or work account), match the Key ID shown.
Look for a printout or saved file from when BitLocker was turned on.

remedies.escalate: Work PCs: IT has the key in your organisation's directory; give them the Key ID shown on screen.

remedies.title: Add a user, or switch between local and Microsoft account
remedies.why: Each person should have their own account; Microsoft accounts sync settings, local accounts stay on this PC.

steps.text: Add someone: Settings › Accounts › Other users › Add account.
Switch your account type: Settings › Accounts › Your info.
Change account type (Standard/Administrator): Settings › Accounts › Other users › the account › Change account type.

remedies.title: Asks for an administrator password I don't have
remedies.why: The change affects the whole computer, and your account is a standard (non-admin) one, which is safer.

steps.text: Ask the computer's owner or IT to approve it, or to install the app for you.
Look for a version of the app that installs for your user only (many installers offer "just me").
At work, use the company's app portal (Company Portal, Self Service) to install approved apps.

remedies.escalate: IT decides admin rights on work computers.
